unit.title: Prepare and produce cakes and puddings products

summary: This unit teaches you to make cakes and puddings for a hotel, villa or bakery: plan and weigh, use the creaming, whisking, rubbing-in and melting methods, bake and test cakes, steam and bake puddings, make custards, and finish, store and label the products safely. It includes Jamaican favourites such as black cake, toto, bulla and sweet potato pudding.

blocks.p: This unit covers the cake and pudding work of a hotel, villa or café kitchen, from reading the recipe to labelling the finished product. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. Cakes and puddings are made from a few simple ingredients, and the **method** (how you mix, how long, how hot) is what decides whether the result is light and moist or heavy and dry.

Jamaican kitchens have their own favourites: the rich black cake at Christmas and weddings, rum cake, toto, bulla, gingerbread, sweet potato pudding and cornmeal pudding. You will learn these alongside the classic sponge and the steamed pudding that guests expect on a hotel menu.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's kitchen. In practical work you make creamed cupcakes and toto, a whisked Swiss roll and a sweet potato pudding. The assessor watches your hygiene, weighing, method, testing, labelling and clean-up as well as the finished products.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph the food, your hands and the work area. Do not photograph a person's face unless they agree and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Cakes and puddings seem safe, but raw egg, raw flour, cream and custard can all carry germs, and a kitchen is full of heat and moving machinery. Safe habits protect the guest and you.

ul: Every food handler in Jamaica must hold a **Food Handler's Permit** from the local health department. Renew it as the department says.
Wear a clean uniform and apron, and cover all your hair. Keep nails short and clean. Take off rings, bracelets and watches (a plain band only if the Centre allows it).
**Wash your hands** with soap and warm water before you start, after handling raw eggs, after touching your face, hair, phone or the bin, and after the toilet. Dry them on a clean paper towel.
Cover cuts with a **blue plaster** and a glove.
If you are ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever, tell your supervisor and do not handle food.
Use **clean eggs with no cracks**, within their date. Keep them in the fridge; take out only what you need.
Never crack eggs on the edge of the mixing bowl: shell and germs fall in. Crack on a flat surface into a small cup first, then add to the bowl.
Wash your hands after cracking eggs. Wash the cup and the surface.

**Do not taste raw cake batter.** Raw egg can carry salmonella, and raw flour can carry germs too, because flour is not heat-treated. Taste only cooked food, or use a clean spoon for a cooked filling.
For desserts that use uncooked egg, use **pasteurised** egg.

Typical figure
Why

Germs multiply fastest. Do not leave food here longer than the Centre's food safety plan allows.

Where it is found in cakes and puddings

Sponges, custards, egg wash, meringue, glazes
Marzipan (almond paste), nut toppings, some chocolate and fillings

ul: If a customer asks whether a cake contains nuts or another allergen, **check the recipe and every label, then tell them what you found**. If you are not sure, ask the chef. Do not guess.
Rum cake and black cake contain alcohol: tell guests who do not drink, and parents buying for children.
Label the allergens on every product for sale.

How you prevent harm

Switch off and wait for the beater to stop before scraping the bowl
Use **dry** oven gloves: heat passes quickly through wet cloth
Warn others with 'hot tray' or 'behind you'
Put hot tins on a heat-proof surface
Steamer or pan of boiling water
Lift the lid **away from you** so that the steam goes the other way
Top up with boiling water, never cold
Keep fingers clear; do not grate the last small piece; use a guard.
Heavy pan, handle turned in, long spoon; never touch or taste it. Hot sugar sticks and burns deeply.

blocks.note: Cool a burn under cool running water for at least 10 minutes. Report all burns and cuts and record them in the accident book.

blocks.p: Switch off and unplug the mixer before you clean it. Wash, rinse, sanitise and dry the bowl and beaters. Wipe spills at once and leave the bench and floor clean, dry and ready for the next person.

ul: **Read the whole recipe** first. You find out what you need, how long each stage takes, and what must be done early (such as softening butter or soaking fruit).
Check the number of portions, and scale if needed.
Check all ingredients are in date, and note the allergens.
Collect the equipment: scales, bowls, sieve, mixer, spatula, tins, baking paper, wire rack.
**Mise en place**: weigh everything in grams, prepare the tins, set the oven shelf and preheat.

blocks.p: Cakes depend on exact ratios of flour, fat, sugar, egg and liquid. Cups and spoons vary: a cup of packed flour can weigh much more than a cup of loose flour. **Weigh in grams** for accuracy, so that every batch comes out the same. Liquids are measured in millilitres in a measuring jug on a flat surface.

head: Ingredient
Its job in the cake
rows: Gives the **structure**. Soft (cake) flour has less protein than strong bread flour, so it gives a soft, tender crumb. **Self-raising flour** has a raising agent already mixed in.
Sweetness, browning of the crust, moisture; helps trap air when creamed with fat.
Tenderness, moisture and flavour; when creamed it holds tiny air bubbles.
Trap air when beaten; bind fat and liquid; **set** when heated, which gives the cake its shape; add colour and flavour.
Makes the cake rise by giving off carbon dioxide gas. Baking powder works when wet and heated. **Bicarbonate of soda** needs an acid, such as molasses, buttermilk or lime juice, to work.
Binds, and gives steam; it dissolves the sugar and activates the raising agent.
Nutmeg, cinnamon, ginger, allspice (pimento), vanilla, rum essence.

blocks.p: Eggs and fat both hold the air that the whisk or beater puts in. The raising agent gives extra lift. Heat sets the egg and the flour, and the shape is fixed.

head: Tool
Use
rows: Weigh in grams; measure liquids in millilitres.
Take out lumps, mix the raising agent through the flour, add air.
Scrape the bowl; fold in flour.
Fold in flour without knocking out the air.
Cake tins, loaf tins, Swiss roll tray, pudding basin
Baking paper, brush and a little fat
Cool cakes so that steam escapes.
Test whether a cake or pudding is baked.
Spread icing and loosen cakes from tins.
Steamer or large pan with a lid and trivet

ul: **Grease** the tin with a thin layer of fat, and **line** the base (and sides for rich cakes) with baking paper, so that the cake turns out whole.
For a Swiss roll, line the tray with paper and lightly grease it.
**Preheat** the oven so that it is at the right heat when the batter goes in. A cake that goes into a cool oven rises badly.
Put the cake in the **middle** of the oven, away from the walls. Use the heat the recipe and the oven maker say. Ovens differ, so learn your own oven and use a thermometer if you can.

blocks.note: These are typical ranges only. Always follow the recipe and the oven maker's instructions, and use your instructor's advice for the Centre's oven.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V at 50 Hz, with 220 V for some heavy equipment. Check that a mixer is made for its socket, keep cables off wet floors, and report any damaged plug.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: There are four main ways of mixing a cake. Each puts air into the mix, or combines the ingredients, in a different way. The recipe tells you which method to use; your job is to follow it exactly.

head: Method
How air gets in
Examples
Qualities
rows: Fat and sugar beaten together until pale and fluffy
Victoria sandwich, butter cake, cupcakes, black cake
Eggs and sugar whisked to a foam
Very light, little or no fat; dries out soon
Fat rubbed into flour; some air from lifting
Fat, sugar and syrup or molasses warmed together
Dense, moist, sticky; improves after a day or two

flow: Weigh everything; soften the fat; line the tins; preheat the oven
Cream the fat and sugar until the mix is **pale, light and fluffy**
Beat the eggs lightly and add them a **little at a time**, beating well after each addition
Sift the flour (with the raising agent) and fold it in gently with a metal spoon or spatula
Add any milk, fruit or flavour; the mix should drop off the spoon
Share the mix into the tins, level the tops and bake

ul: **Why cream?** The sharp sugar crystals cut tiny air pockets into the fat, and these expand in the oven.

**Why add the egg a little at a time?** Cold egg added all at once makes the mix **curdle** (split). The fat and the liquid separate, and the cake is heavy. If it begins to curdle, add a spoonful of the flour and keep beating.
**Why fold the flour?** Beating it in hard knocks out the air and develops gluten, making the cake tough. Fold by cutting down through the mix and turning it over, rotating the bowl.
**Victoria sandwich:** equal weights of butter, caster sugar, eggs and self-raising flour. Example: if the eggs, out of their shells, weigh 180 g, use 180 g each of butter, sugar and flour.

flow: Line a Swiss roll tray; preheat the oven to a hot heat
Whisk the eggs and sugar (over a pan of hot water, or with a mixer) until very thick and pale
Check the **ribbon stage**: lift the whisk and a trail stays on the surface for a few seconds
Sift the flour and fold it in very gently, so that the air is not lost
Spread the mix evenly in the tray
Bake quickly until golden and springy
Turn out onto sugared paper, trim the edges, spread with jam and roll up while warm

ul: A whisked sponge has no raising agent, so the air in the egg foam is all the lift. **Any loss of air** makes it flat.
Do not open the oven in the first half of baking.
Roll the Swiss roll while it is warm, so that it does not crack. If it has cooled and cracks, it was overbaked or dry.

blocks.p: Rub cold fat into the flour with the fingertips until it looks like **fine breadcrumbs**. Then stir in the sugar, fruit and spices, and add just enough egg and milk to make a stiff mix. Rock cakes are a typical example: they are spooned in rough heaps onto a tray, not poured. They are best eaten the same day.

Warm the fat, sugar, syrup or molasses together in a pan until melted: do not boil. Cool a little. Then mix the melted ingredients into the dry ingredients (flour, spices and bicarbonate of soda) and add the egg and milk. The mix is thin and is poured into the tin. Gingerbread and bulla are made this way.

ul: **Molasses** is acid, so it reacts with **bicarbonate of soda** to give gas that lifts the cake, and it makes the colour dark.
Do not boil the mixture: too much heat changes the sugar and the cake can be hard.
These cakes improve if stored for a day, when they become moister.
Always switch off and wait for the beater to stop before you scrape the bowl or put in a spoon.
Scrape the sides and the bottom of the bowl once or twice so that nothing stays unmixed.

blocks.h: Black cake (Jamaican Christmas and wedding cake)

blocks.p: Jamaican **black cake** (also called rum cake or fruit cake) is a rich, dark, moist fruit cake, made with dried fruit that has been soaked for days or weeks in rum and red wine. It is served at Christmas and at weddings.

flow: Weeks ahead: chop or mince the dried fruit (raisins, currants, prunes, cherries, mixed peel) and soak it in rum and wine
On baking day: line a deep tin with two layers of baking paper, and wrap the outside with brown paper to protect the sides
Cream butter and brown sugar until light
Add the eggs a little at a time
Add the soaked fruit, a little browning (burnt sugar), mixed spice and vanilla
Fold in the flour
Bake slowly at a low heat for several hours, as the recipe and oven maker say
Test with a skewer, then cool in the tin
Pour over a little rum while it is warm, wrap and store

ul: **Why soak the fruit?** Soaking softens the fruit and gives the cake a deep flavour. It also keeps the cake moist. The fruit does not burn on the outside of the cake.
**Why bake at a low heat for a long time?** A large, dense cake must cook through to the middle without the outside burning.
**Browning** is burnt sugar. It gives the cake its dark colour and a slightly bitter flavour. Use only the amount in the recipe.
A rich cake cools in its tin, so that it does not break.
Wrapped well and kept cool, a rich rum-soaked cake keeps for weeks; many families make it well ahead.

blocks.p: A **rum cake** is a butter cake that is soaked, after baking, with a syrup made of sugar, water, butter and rum. Add the syrup **while the cake is still warm**, so that it soaks in. Pour slowly in small amounts and let each go in before adding more.

**Toto** is a small, sweet, spiced coconut cake, often baked in a tray and cut into squares. It is made from grated coconut, flour, brown sugar, butter, baking powder, nutmeg and other spices, and is sold in school tuck shops and bakeries. Follow the Centre's recipe for the method (creaming or rubbing-in), and bake until golden and firm. Cut it into even portions when it is cool.

**Bulla** is a flat, round, dense cake, made by the melting method with wet sugar or molasses, ginger and bicarbonate of soda. It is often eaten with a slice of pear (the Jamaican word for avocado) or cheese. The acid in the molasses and the bicarbonate of soda give it a little lift.

Gingerbread is made by the melting method with molasses and ginger. Other popular Jamaican products include grater cake (grated coconut and sugar), cornmeal pudding and sweet potato pudding (see the section on puddings), and spiced buns.

blocks.note: Kitchens in Jamaica get very busy before Christmas, with large orders for black cake. Plan the soaking months ahead, label every tin with the date, and keep the cakes cool and dry. Keep alcohol labelled on the box, because some customers do not drink it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

Likely cause
Prevention
rows: Mix too soft; fruit very wet; oven too hot at first
Drain wet fruit; use the right amount of liquid; fold fruit in gently
Oven too hot; no paper lining
Low heat; double lining and brown paper
Too much raising agent; oven door opened early
Weigh carefully; keep the door shut

blocks.h: Do not open the oven door early

blocks.p: In the first part of baking, the cake is still thin and soft. Cold air from an open door makes it sink. Wait until the cake has risen and is just beginning to set before you check it.

blocks.h: How to test that a cake is baked

head: Cake
Test
rows: Press the top lightly with a finger: it should **spring back**. It also begins to shrink from the sides of the tin.
Rich fruit cake, pudding, loaf cake
Push a clean **skewer** into the middle: it should come out clean. If wet mix clings to it, bake longer.
The top is golden and springs back.
Set and firm, with a golden top, and a skewer comes out clean (a soft custard-like layer on top is normal).

head: Fault
Likely cause
How to prevent it
rows: Too much raising agent; oven door opened early; taken out before it was baked; oven too cool
Weigh the raising agent; keep the door shut; test before removing
Risen to a peak and cracked
Oven too hot; shelf too high; mix too stiff
Check the oven heat; use the middle shelf
Not creamed enough; eggs curdled; flour beaten in hard; too little raising agent
Cream until pale and fluffy; add egg slowly; fold in gently
Overbaked; too much flour; too little liquid or fat
Mix too soft; fruit wet or heavy
Dry the fruit; check the mix
Oven too cool; baked too briefly
Mix overbeaten after the flour went in
Tin not greased or lined; turned out too soon or too late
Grease and line; leave a few minutes, then turn out

ul: Leave most cakes in the tin for **a few minutes**, so that they firm up and do not break.
Then turn them onto a **wire rack**, so that steam escapes and the base does not go soggy.
Rich fruit cakes cool in the tin.
Do not ice, fill with cream or wrap a cake until it is **completely cool**, or the icing melts and the wrapping makes the cake sweat and go mouldy.

flow: Grease the pudding basin well; put jam or syrup in the bottom if the recipe says
Make the sponge mix by the creaming method
Fill the basin about **two-thirds full**, so there is room to rise
Cover with greaseproof paper and foil with a **pleat** folded across the middle, and tie it with string, making a string handle
Stand the basin in a steamer, or on a trivet in a large pan, with boiling water about halfway up the basin; put the lid on
Steam for the time the recipe says, keeping the water simmering
Check often that the water has not boiled away; top up with **boiling** water
Lift the lid **away from you**; use dry gloves
Test with a skewer, loosen the edge and turn out onto a warm plate

ul: **Why a pleat?** The pudding rises and needs space under the lid. Without a pleat the cover bursts or the pudding is dense.
**Why boiling water for topping up?** Cold water stops the steaming and makes the pudding heavy.
A pan that boils dry can burn through and cause a fire. Never leave steaming puddings unattended.

head: Pudding
Main ingredients
How it is cooked
rows: Grated sweet potato, coconut milk, brown sugar, a little flour or cornmeal, melted butter, nutmeg, cinnamon, vanilla, raisins
Baked in a greased tin in a moderate oven until set and golden; a soft custard-like layer on top is normal
Cornmeal, coconut milk, sugar, spices, raisins; sometimes sweet potato or pumpkin
Buttered bread, dried fruit, egg custard
Layered in a dish, covered with custard, baked

ul: **Peel and grate sweet potato with care.** Keep fingers clear of the grater; do not grate the last small piece.
Sweet potato pudding is done when it is set and firm, the top is golden, and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool it before you cut it. A warm pudding crumbles. Cut it into even portions.
Label the allergens: wheat and milk, and any nuts in toppings.

blocks.p: A custard is a mix of milk, egg and sugar, which sets when heated gently. Eggs **scramble** if heated too hard.

head: Kind
How to cook it
Key rule
rows: Heat milk; whisk it onto egg yolks and sugar; cook over low heat, stirring all the time, until it coats the back of a spoon
**Never let it boil**: the egg scrambles and the sauce curdles. Strain into a cold bowl as soon as it is cooked.
Pour into a dish; stand it in a tray of hot water (a **bain-marie**); bake slowly
The water makes the heat gentle, so it sets smoothly without curdling or bubbles.
Cornflour mixed with a little cold milk, then stirred into hot milk
Stir all the time and cook until thick.

ul: A custard that is a little too hot at the end can be saved by taking it off the heat and stirring in cold milk at once, but a scrambled one cannot.
Cover custard with cling film touching the surface so that it does not form a skin. Cool quickly, and chill at 5 °C or below.
Custard and cream puddings are high-risk foods: keep them covered in the fridge and use them within the time the Centre's food safety plan allows.

blocks.note: A bain-marie is a tray of hot water. A pudding dish is put inside it in the oven. Carry it level and with dry gloves: the hot water can spill and scald. Pour the water into the tray once it is in the oven.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Make sure the cake is **completely cool**
Trim the top level and brush off loose crumbs
Spread a layer of jam and buttercream or cream between the layers
Cover the sides and top with a thin **crumb coat** and chill it
Add the final coat and smooth it with a palette knife dipped in hot water and dried
Decorate neatly and simply: piping, fruit, toasted coconut or a dusting of icing sugar

head: Icing or topping
What it is
Notes
rows: Soft butter beaten with icing sugar (about twice the weight of the butter) and a little milk
Put it on a cool cake only, or it melts and slides off.
Icing sugar and a little water or juice
Quick; sets with a thin, shiny crust.
Icing sugar and egg white (or a substitute), sets hard
Used on Jamaican wedding and Christmas fruit cakes, often over marzipan.
Chilled cream, whipped to soft or firm peaks
Needs chilling: cream cakes must be kept at 5 °C or below.

ul: Mark the cake into **even portions** with a portion marker or guide before you cut, so that every customer gets the same amount and the cost is controlled.
Cut with a clean, **hot, dry** knife and wipe it between cuts.
Present each portion or the whole cake on a clean board or stand, with a label showing the name, price and allergens.

head: Product
Storage
rows: Plain sponge, loaf cakes, toto, bulla
Clean, airtight container in a cool, dry place, away from strong smells and pests.
Wrapped well in paper and foil in a cool, dry place; keeps for weeks.
Cream or custard cakes, cut puddings, cold desserts
Covered, in the fridge at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says.

blocks.p: Label every tray, tin and container with the **name of the product, the date made, a use-by date and the allergens**. Use stock in date order: **first in, first out**.

blocks.note: In a hot Jamaican kitchen, cakes with buttercream or cream go soft and spoil fast. Keep them chilled until the last minute, and carry them to an event in a cool box.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Wash, rinse, sanitise and dry the bowls, beaters, tins and tools. Switch off and unplug the mixer.
Wipe and clean the benches and the oven door; sweep and mop the floor.
Report faulty equipment and low stock to your supervisor.

c1.title: A birthday cake order in Portmore
c1.text: Trainee Janelle makes a two-layer Victoria sandwich for a customer's birthday in Portmore. She beats all four eggs into the creamed butter and sugar at once, and the mix splits. She rescues it, bakes the cakes, and when the layers come out she wants to spread buttercream on them at once because the customer is waiting. One cake has risen to a cracked peak. The customer also asks for cream between the layers and wants to collect it in three hours.

c2.title: Black cake before Christmas in Christiana
c2.text: A bakery in Christiana takes orders for black cake. The head baker, Mr Delroy Francis, soaked the chopped raisins, prunes and cherries in rum and red wine for three weeks. His trainee Nadine bakes the cake at a low heat for about three hours. At two and a half hours she pushes a skewer into the middle and it comes out with wet mix on it. A customer who does not drink alcohol asks whether the cake is suitable for her son's school party.

c3.title: Toto and bulla for a tuck shop in Spanish Town
c3.text: Trainees at the Centre's kitchen bake toto and bulla for a school tuck shop in Spanish Town. Garfield makes the bulla by warming wet sugar, molasses and margarine in a pan, then mixing in flour, ginger and bicarbonate of soda. His first mix is very thick and smells scorched because the pan boiled. Sherene bakes toto in a tray and cuts it into squares straight from the oven. The squares crumble.

c4.title: A steamed pudding at a Treasure Beach villa
c4.text: Chef Alicia is teaching a trainee to steam a jam sponge pudding for the guests of a villa in Treasure Beach. The trainee fills the basin to the top, covers it with flat paper and foil, and puts it in a pan of boiling water that comes to the rim of the basin. After an hour the water level has dropped and the pan is almost dry. At the end she lifts the lid towards her face.

c5.title: Sweet potato pudding and custard at a Port Antonio guesthouse
c5.text: At a guesthouse in Port Antonio, trainee Kemar grates sweet potato for a pudding and cuts his knuckle on the grater. He also makes egg custard sauce for the pudding: he heats the milk, whisks it into the yolks and sugar, then boils the sauce to thicken it quickly. It scrambles. The pudding is baked until golden and firm, and a guest asks whether it can be served for dessert at 7 p.m., though it was baked at noon.

questions.q: Janelle's mix split after she added all the eggs at once. What is the usual way to recover it?
o: Add a spoonful of flour and keep beating
Add a little cold water and stir gently
Stop beating and put it in the fridge for a while
Add extra baking powder to make it rise
questions.why: Cold egg added all at once makes the fat and liquid separate. A spoonful of the flour helps bind them again; next time add the egg a little at a time.

questions.q: Why should Janelle not spread buttercream on the layers as soon as they come out?
o: The buttercream would be too sweet on a warm cake
The cake would absorb the butter and go dry
The warm cake would fall apart as she cut it
The buttercream would melt and slide off
questions.why: Warm cake melts butter-based icing, so it slides off. Cool the cake completely on a wire rack before filling or icing.

questions.q: What most likely made one cake rise to a cracked peak?
o: The oven was too hot, or the tin was too high
The mix had too little raising agent in it, so it cracked
The butter and sugar were creamed for much too long
The cake was left to cool in the tin for too long a time
questions.why: A very hot oven sets the outside before the middle has finished rising, and the middle pushes up and cracks. Use the middle shelf and the right heat.

questions.q: The customer wants fresh cream between the layers and will collect in three hours. What should Janelle do?
o: Fill the cake now and keep it on the bench under a cloth
Fill it now and put it in the warm cupboard to set
Fill it just before collection and keep it chilled until then
Fill it now and keep it near the oven door so that it stays soft
questions.why: Fresh cream is a high-risk food, and must be kept at 5 °C or below. Fill the cake close to collection and keep it chilled, or keep it in the fridge once filled.

questions.q: What is the main reason for soaking the dried fruit for black cake for weeks?
o: To make the fruit sink to the bottom of the cake
To stop the cake from rising too much in the hot oven
To make the fruit smaller so that it can be mixed in easily
To soften the fruit and give the cake a rich flavour
questions.why: Long soaking softens the fruit and fills it with the flavour of the rum and wine, so that the cake is rich and moist. The fruit does not dry out or burn in the oven.

questions.q: Nadine's skewer comes out with wet mix on it. What should she do?
o: Take the cake out, as it will finish cooking while it cools
Raise the oven heat so that the middle cooks faster
Leave it for a further 15–20 minutes and test again
Cover the top with foil and turn the oven off
questions.why: A skewer with wet mix means the middle is not set. A rich cake needs more time at a low heat; raising the heat burns the outside while the middle stays raw.

questions.q: Why is a large black cake baked at a low heat for several hours?
o: The fruit must dry out slowly in the oven over the hours
The middle cooks through without the outside burning
A low heat makes the cake rise higher than a hot oven would
The rum evaporates quickly at a high heat, so it must be low
questions.why: A big, dense cake takes a long time to heat through. A low heat lets the middle cook before the outside burns.

questions.q: The customer's son will be at a school party. What should the bakery tell her?
o: The alcohol cooks out completely, so it is safe for children
Black cake is only for adults and cannot be sold for parties
It contains rum and wine, so it may not suit a child's party
The cake is safe if the label does not show any allergens
questions.why: Black cake is soaked in rum and wine and often fed with rum afterwards, so some alcohol remains. Tell customers honestly, and label it, so they can decide.

questions.q: Garfield's bulla mix is very thick and smells scorched. What went wrong?
o: The bicarbonate of soda was added before the flour
The pan boiled instead of just being warmed
The molasses was too cold to mix in
The ginger was added too late
questions.why: In the melting method, the fat, sugar and molasses are only warmed until melted. Boiling changes the sugar and makes the mix thick and scorched.

questions.q: What does the molasses do in a bulla, together with the bicarbonate of soda?
o: It reacts with it to give gas that lifts the cake
It keeps the bicarbonate from tasting bitter in the finished cake
It sets the cake firmly so that it does not rise at all
It dissolves the flour so that the whole mix is smooth
questions.why: Molasses is acid. Bicarbonate of soda needs an acid to give off carbon dioxide, so the two together give some lift and also colour the cake dark.

questions.q: Why do Sherene's toto squares crumble?
o: They were cut while still hot, before they firmed up
They were baked at too low a heat for the time given
They had too much coconut in them for the amount of flour
They were cut with a knife that was too sharp for the job
questions.why: A hot toto is soft and breaks apart. Let it cool and firm up in the tray, then cut it into even portions with a clean knife.

questions.q: Why should the basin not be filled to the top?
o: The pudding needs room to rise under the cover
The steam must reach the top of the basin to cook it
The pudding would be too heavy to lift out of the pan
The sponge would be too hard to turn out afterwards
questions.why: A sponge pudding rises as it steams. Fill the basin about two-thirds full and fold a pleat in the cover so that there is space.

questions.q: The pan is nearly dry after an hour. What is the right action?
o: Add cold water from the tap so the pan cools down
Leave it, because the pudding is already cooked
Turn up the heat so that the pudding finishes sooner
Top up with boiling water, and check the level often
questions.why: The water must not boil away: a dry pan can burn and cause a fire. Top up with boiling water, because cold water stops the steaming.

questions.q: Why is lifting the steamer lid towards her face dangerous?
o: The steam can scald her face and hands
The lid is too heavy to lift without help
The paper cover will stick to the lid
The pudding will sink if the lid is tilted
questions.why: Escaping steam is hotter than boiling water and burns severely. Lift the lid away from you, so that the steam goes the other way, and wear dry gloves.

questions.q: Kemar cuts his knuckle on the grater. What should he do before he handles any more food?
o: Rinse the cut under the tap and carry on with a glove on
Treat the cut, cover it with a blue plaster and glove, then report it
Wipe the blood off with a cloth and carry on grating the sweet potato
Put on a bandage from the first aid box and keep working on the pudding
questions.why: A cut must be cleaned and covered with a waterproof blue plaster and a glove, so that it cannot get into the food. Report it and write it in the accident book.

questions.q: Why did Kemar's custard sauce scramble?
o: The milk was not hot enough before it was whisked in
The sauce was boiled, which cooks the egg into lumps
He used egg yolks instead of the whole egg
He stirred the sauce too much while it cooked
questions.why: Egg proteins set and curdle above about 85 °C. A custard sauce must be cooked gently over low heat, stirring, until it coats the back of a spoon, and never boiled.

questions.q: Kemar wants to bake a plain egg custard for the guesthouse. How should he cook it?
o: On the top shelf of a hot oven, so that the top browns well
In a dish standing in a tray of hot water, baked slowly
In a deep pan of boiling water on the hob, with the lid on
In a dish on the floor of the oven, with the oven door left open
questions.why: A bain-marie makes the heat gentle and even, so that the custard sets smoothly without curdling or bubbles.

questions.q: The pudding was baked at noon and will be served at 7 p.m. How should it be kept?
o: Left on the bench, so that it stays soft for the guests
Cooled, covered and chilled, then served as the plan says
Kept in a warm cupboard until it is needed for the dessert
Put in the fridge uncovered while it is still hot from the oven
questions.why: A pudding left warm for hours sits in the danger zone. Cool it quickly, cover it, chill it at 5 °C or below, and serve or reheat it as the Centre's food safety plan says.

questions.q: A Victoria sandwich uses equal weights of butter, sugar, eggs and flour. Four eggs weigh 240 g. How much butter is needed?
questions.why: In a Victoria sandwich, every main ingredient weighs the same as the eggs. So the butter is 240 g, and so are the sugar and the flour.

questions.q: Which pair of cakes are both made by the melting method?
o: Gingerbread and bulla
Rock cakes and scones
Swiss roll and gingerbread
Victoria sandwich and bulla
questions.why: Gingerbread and bulla both have fat, sugar and molasses warmed together first. Rock cakes and scones are rubbed in; a Swiss roll is whisked; a Victoria sandwich is creamed.
